newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel police open high-level corruption probe.
newsitem.headline: Israel police open high-level corruption probe.

text.p: Israeli police launched an investigation on Sunday into allegations of high-level corruption which politicians said could bring down Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's seven-month-old government.

Justice officials ordered the investigation into Netanyahu's ill-fated appointment of an attorney general days after Israel's Channel One alleged the appointment was part of a political deal to win a plea bargain for Aryeh Deri, a key coalition party leader on trial for corruption.
State prosecutor and acting Attorney General Edna Arbel ordered an investigation on Sunday after talks with police.
Police Commissioner Assaf Hefetz appointed a seven-member team to lead the investigation which could summon Netanyahu and top officials for questioning.
"Despite the sensitivity of the investigation, the Israeli police can be trusted to conduct it quickly and fairly," Hefetz told a news conference.
Hefetz said police investigators turned to the television to review the evidence upon which it based its allegations.

State-owned Channel One started the storm last week by alleging that Jerusalem lawyer Roni Bar-On was appointed attorney general after promising to arrange a plea bargain for Deri, whose 10-member Shas party is a key component in Netanyahu's coalition.

The television said Deri, on trial since 1993 on a range of corruption charges, conditioned his party's support for Israel's Hebron deal with the PLO on Bar-On's being appointed attorney general after the post opened up.

Seven ministers in Netanyahu's 18-member cabinet voted against the Hebron agreement, reached after months of acrimonious negotiations with the PLO. Opposition by Shas's two ministers might have put the agreement in jeopardy.
"If there was any kind of bargain, I recommend to everyone involved to admit it and resign because this is an unprecedented crime," said cabinet minister Natan Sharansky.
"If these allegations are true, I am very concerned about our whole democratic regime," he told Israel Radio.

Asked on television if the government could stay in office if the allegations proved accurate, Internal Security Minister Avigdor Kahalani said: "If the affair is in fact as it appears, at least, there is no doubt that this government has no place."

Bar-On, an activist in Netanyahu's Likud party, resigned within 12 hours of taking office earlier this month under public criticism he was a legal lightweight. Bar-On, Deri and Netanyahu denied the television's allegations.
Netanyahu called for a police investigation as public discourse centred on the validity of the report and the rights of journalists to keep secret the identity of their sources.

"We will take this all the way. I'm not concerned, I'm not scared and I'm not worried. We will protect our sources but will act within the confines of the law," said Rafik Halabi, editor of Channel One's nightly newscast.
Police commissioner Hefetz said the television might be obliged to reveal its sources.
"It could well be that the media shelter will need to be put to the test," he told Channel Two television.
Shas deputy minister Shlomo Ben-Izri said Israel Television should have taken any information it might have obtained directly to the police rather than airing it.

"Why didn't your reporter immediately take this information to the police? Is it her role to judge and to spill people's blood? Is the television Israel's national investigator?" Ben-Izri told Israel Radio.
